summary:
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's record of the global history of criminalisation dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.

The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the United States Department of State's 2015 Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands. It recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, enforced disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses, and it listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence among the significant problems it identified.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 United States Department of State report named prison conditions as a significant problem in the Marshall Islands. Detention is the setting in which that finding would bear on a visitor directly, and it stands alongside the report's finding of no recorded LGBT-specific abuses.

The Pacific Sexual & Gender Diversity Network profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese person who co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, regarded as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. That the initiative is recorded as the first of its kind indicates how few established organisations a visitor could turn to for community contact.

Corruption is recorded in the same report as a significant national problem, a factor that touches official encounters generally rather than LGBT status specifically.
localsOnly:
Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese person, co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, regarded as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. Kaminaga is also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and served as a youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.

The 2015 United States Department of State report records domestic violence as a significant problem inside the country, alongside corruption and prison conditions. No LGBT-specific abuse was reported to that mission for the period covered.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition in the Marshall Islands. Whether a resident or visitor can obtain a change of gender marker on a Marshallese passport or other national document, and by what procedure, remains unresolved here. What can be said is that border and screening officials will work from the marker on the document presented at entry, since no local amendment route is documented.

Entry and visa requirements are not covered by any source in the inventory, and no source addresses how Marshallese border officials treat a foreign passport carrying a gender marker changed in another country. That handling is not sourced.

Human Dignity Trust supplies the 2005 decriminalisation date, but no source in the inventory identifies the statute repealed or the body that repealed it.

The 2015 United States Department of State Human Rights Report is the most recent official country reporting available here. Anything after 2015, including later changes to law, policy or enforcement practice, is not sourced in this inventory.
